title: 150+ hours into game dev and I’ve become extremely efficient at creating future work
author: Cautious_Material_40
selftext:
Been building this for the past couple of months and recently migrated the project from a browser-based setup over to Unity. That switch has helped a ton, especially with getting systems built, tested, and iterated on faster.

Right now, the game uses a mix of AI-assisted assets, purchased pixel art, commissioned work, and placeholders, while all of the coding is done through AI. I’ve had it build a handful of tools that let me tweak certain values and settings myself, but the actual code is still handled entirely through AI.

A lot of the current enemies are basically test dummies while I experiment with different behaviors, attacks, and animations to figure out what actually feels fun before investing more into final art.

The core gameplay is starting to feel pretty solid. Combat and traversal are both in a decent place mechanically, but they still need more polish, balancing, and situations that actually give all of those mechanics a reason to exist.

Of course, every time I get one system feeling good, I seem to come up with three more things I want to add, so the scope management is going extremely well.

There’s still a ton left to do, but I’ve been having a lot of fun with it and learning a ridiculous amount along the way. I’m also way more comfortable working in Unity now than I was when I started.

I’m somewhere around 150+ hours into the project at this point, there’s no end in sight, and apparently none of those hours made me any better at actually playing it.

Curious what other AI-assisted devs think of the direction it’s heading.

And to the AI game-dev haters who made it this far: thank you for contributing to my engagement metrics. ❤️

comments.author: Cosmonan
comments.body: Good job! Animations are pretty smooth, and that's one of the most difficult parts of AI game-dev. I'm sure as the assets get refined you won't even be able to tell AI was used. Keep up!

replies.author: Cautious_Material_40
replies.body:
Thanks! The player character was hand made pixel art that I purchased. A handful of the enemies are ai generated, as well as some of the set mechanic pieces.  
I started the playable character with AI animating but it was just too much to get it right, and even then it was choppy.  
Moved to purchasing pixel art assets and thats been really helpful in building out the foundation of the game.

replies.author: phiiiiiiii
replies.body: How much did you spend on that set of sprite? Did you buy the backdrop art as well?

replies.author: Cautious_Material_40
replies.body:
$15 for the sprite, which honestly floored me considering the quality. Huge shoutout to the pixel artist! [https://merakintsugi.itch.io/platformer-character-pack](https://merakintsugi.itch.io/platformer-character-pack)  
I picked up the tileset from [itch.io](http://itch.io) as well, but I built the stage itself by hand. AI has actually been pretty terrible at laying out anything decent with a tileset, so level design has been one of the things I’ve mostly handled myself.

replies.author: phiiiiiiii
replies.body:
Oh I see, so it was an asset pack and not commissioned work. I was wondering if you have a particular vision for character design and want to have it hand-drawn by commission, how much would it cost.

By the way, AI generated asset is not too bad, but requires a lot of harness to maintain consistency. GPT Image has been pretty good with this, although it still have a long way to go.

replies.author: Cautious_Material_40
replies.body:
I've been finding a varying amount of prices for different artists. I'm using Fiverr to reach out to pixel artists and see what artist and varying skill levels can do work for x amount of dollars.  
This animation itself is 12 frames, and typically im finding a 12 frame animation can cost a range of $50-$200. So around that much.

replies.author: phiiiiiiii
replies.body:
Good to know, thank you. Did you give the commissioned artist an AI-generated concept art of your character, or did you give them artistic control?

I've found that a set of sprites generated through AI (4 standing sprites and 16 moving frames) can cost between $7 to $15 using GPT-image 2.5. But, the output, while passable, can be difficult to keep consistent. The advantage is instant gratification & trial and error, so really good for prototyping.

replies.author: Cautious_Material_40
replies.body:
Yes, I gave my artist a couple of ideas, which he iterated on, and I helped along with ai generated art.   
I actually have a pretty substantial part of the game built with an ai generated character, but it is just no match for good ole' fashioned human drawn pixel art.

replies.author: phiiiiiiii
replies.body: I see. Do you think it's efficient to prototype with AI placeholders first, then have artists replace them with human art?

replies.author: Cautious_Material_40
replies.body:
I started with AI art, and most of my time was spent generating that art, and not actually building the game. I got to a point where the things I wanted to program, AI art was not working for me, so I began to look elsewhere.  
Protyping art is definitely helpful, and spurred me to actually start my game dev journey and helped build the foundatin of the game.  
But I havent found it to look as good as i wanted it to, and it was frustratingly challenging to get the little quality that i did from it.  
So take that as you will.

replies.author: Lextrot
replies.body: What harnesses do you use/recommend?

replies.author: Cautious_Material_40
replies.body: I've mostly been using Claude Code and Codex, with MCP hooked into Unity. I'm still pretty new to AI-assisted game dev though, so I'm definitely experimenting with what works best.

replies.author: Cautious_Material_40
replies.body:
Yeah, it actually started out as a pretty straightforward Mega Man X-inspired game. I may have borrowed a few sounds from it early on too, but I’m in the process of replacing those now.

As I kept building, I started experimenting more with melee combat and ended up really liking the direction it took. I still want to keep that core Mega Man X feel, but I’m also trying to give it its own identity instead of just recreating the same thing.

comments.author: ectoblob
comments.body:
Character feels oversized compared to tile size of level. Also color palette of character sort of clashes with environment style. Some of those aerial attacks look like character was grounded, otherwise nice looking moves and effects. Background elements flicker, it looks like you have seams there, use padding if those are tiles.   
  
Character style feels more like some high fantasy settings, but then you have those Metal Slug like enemies, and mostly fantasy past looking environments, of course it could be part of the story, but it isn't quite obvious here.  
  
Anyway, mocking those who may not use AI feels childish - this kinds of platformer/metroidvania/roguelite platformer games are mostly about balancing of visual style and movements, it isn't that much about code anyway, more about stylistic choices.

comments.author: Cautious_Material_40

Thanks for the feedback.
I hadn't realized the 100+ hours I spent working on the coding didnt really matter.
Good thing you graced me with your wisdom so I dont waste anymore of my time!
